title: Should organ donation be opt-out?

turns.speaker: Bea
turns.text: Opt-out came in three years ago and the transplant numbers have barely moved. I'd assumed they'd jump.

turns.speaker: Hamed
turns.text: Everyone assumed that. The countries held up as proof, like Spain, changed the law decades before the numbers rose.

turns.speaker: Hamed
turns.text: Specialist coordinators in every hospital. Someone trained whose actual job is that conversation with a family at the worst hour of their life.

turns.speaker: Bea
turns.text: Because in practice the family is still asked, opt-out or not.

turns.speaker: Lorna
turns.text: Which is the thing nobody says out loud when the law passes. No surgeon is going to proceed over a grieving family's objection.

turns.speaker: Lorna
turns.text: So the legal default matters far less than how that conversation goes.

turns.speaker: Hamed
turns.text: Although the default does help the conversation. It shifts it from asking permission to confirming a decision already made.

turns.speaker: Bea
turns.text: That's a real difference in a room like that.

turns.speaker: Lorna
turns.text: The objection I take seriously is consent. Silence is being read as agreement, and some people never heard about the change at all.

turns.speaker: Hamed
turns.text: The register answers that partly. You can record a refusal and it's binding.

turns.speaker: Lorna
turns.text: Which is the whole objection in four words, really.

points: Three years after opt-out donation was introduced, transplant numbers have barely changed.
Hamed notes countries cited as successes changed their law decades before donation rates rose.
The decisive factor was specialist coordinators in hospitals trained to hold conversations with bereaved families.
Families are still consulted regardless of the legal default, since surgeons will not override objections.
Hamed argues the default still helps by reframing the conversation from seeking permission to confirming an existing decision.
Lorna's remaining objection is that silence is treated as consent when many people never learned of the change, which the refusal register only partly answers.
